title: The numbers that quietly went wrong
teaches: Checking data before it is published: contracts and control totals, invariant and statistical checks, quarantine, write-audit-publish, and data SLIs

blocks.text: On Friday 2 October 2020, during the second wave of Covid in England, the UK's daily figures showed about 7,000 new positive tests. Over that weekend the figures jumped: almost 13,000 on Saturday and almost 23,000 on Sunday. The jump was not a sudden rise in infections. On 4 October Public Health England announced that 15,841 positive results from the period between 25 September and 2 October had not been included in the published counts, and that their details had not reached the contact-tracing system on time.

The commercial laboratories sent their results as CSV files, plain text with one line per record. Part of the process that collected them loaded each file into a Microsoft Excel template in the older XLS format, which holds at most 65,536 rows. Each case took up many rows, so a template could hold only about 1,400 cases, and when a file had more, the rows beyond the limit were dropped without any error.[^xls] The people tested had been told their results; what was delayed was the national count and the tracing of their contacts. Nothing in the process compared the number of results a laboratory had sent with the number that arrived.
Before reading on, consider which single check would have caught this on the first day.

In this lesson, we will design the checks that stand between a nightly build of the world map from lesson P3 and the teams that read it, such as routing, search, rendering and machine learning. A wrong version is worse than a late one. A broken service fails loudly and someone is paged, but a dataset with a region missing or a unit misread looks normal to every system that reads it, and the error spreads into routing graphs, search results and training data before anyone notices.

parts.title: What it must do, and what it need not

blocks.text: **Functional.** The checks must reject malformed input when it arrives, catch outputs that are well formed but wrong, keep rejected records where people can inspect them, and stop a bad version from being published without anyone having to act. Each check must have an owner, and each producer of data must know what it has promised to send.

**Non-functional.** A check must run in minutes, so that a nightly publish is not delayed by hours. False alarms must be rare, about one a month at most, to prevent alert fatigue and routine overrides. The time from a source failure to alerting the designated owner must be under one hour.

**Out of scope.** We will not design the remediation of invalid source data, which remains the responsibility of the upstream team, or the evaluation of models trained on the data, which is addressed in lesson P1.

Most data faults occur where one team hands data to another, so our design begins there. A **data contract** is a written agreement, kept in version control beside the pipeline code, between a team that produces a dataset and the teams that consume it. It specifies the schema, the semantic meaning and units of each field, the expected freshness, the expected record volume, and who receives an alert when a check fails. The producer executes the contract checks in its own build pipeline before sending any data, catching most mistakes before they leave the team that created them.

The contract should also require a **control total**[^batch-totals] with every delivery: the number of records, and a checksum computed over them, sent separately from the data itself. The receiver counts the records it loaded and compares the result with the transmitted total. That single check would have caught the Covid-19 reporting failure on its first day, when only about 1,400 cases were loaded from a file that held several thousand. The receiver also verifies that every expected delivery arrived, and treats a file without its total, or a total without its file, as a failed delivery.

parts.title: Checks on the way in and on the way out

blocks.text: Checks fall into two kinds. **Invariant checks** test rules that must always hold, and the data either passes or fails. Some apply to each record on its own: every field has the right type, a speed limit is between 5 and 140 km/h or marked as having none, every place is inside some country. These are cheap and exact, and they run at ingestion, on each source as it arrives. Others need the whole built version, so they run in the audit described below: IDs are unique, every road segment's end points exist, every reference points at a record that is there, and the major roads still form one connected network.

Invariant checks cannot see data that is valid record by record and wrong as a whole: a region with half its roads, a day's file from a source that sent yesterday's file again, speeds that are all in range but in the wrong unit for one country. **Statistical checks** compare the output with what is expected: the number of records per region, the distribution of each important field, the share of records that changed since the last version, and the share of IDs retired or newly created, each compared region by region. Two design choices make these work. First, they should judge the size of a change, such as 'the number of roads in this region fell by 12%', against an owner-defined threshold, rather than asking whether a change is statistically significant, because with millions of records almost any change is significant. Measuring a change in units of the region's ordinary night-to-night noise is still a judgement of size, because the threshold then means unusual for this region. If a region's road count moves by about 1% on an ordinary night, one standard deviation is about 1% of its count. Second, the pipeline should compare metrics against two baselines: recent history, which adapts to normal change, and a fixed reference version, which does not adapt and therefore catches a slow drift that recent history would absorb. The fixed reference must itself be refreshed periodically, for example each quarter after a review, to prevent legitimate growth from tripping the threshold.

Some changes reflect legitimate updates. A source adds a country, a new road network opens, or a team renames a category. The design lets the owner of a change **declare** it in advance, specifying the expected effect on counts so that the checks account for the shift rather than raising an alert. Data for machine-learning models needs one more check: that no **feature**, an input column a model learns from, has silently become empty or constant. This silent failure occurs when an upstream field is renamed and the pipeline fills in a default value. A model trained on that data learns to ignore the feature, while the pipeline reports no error.

Checks protect production only if a validation failure stops the publish. The **write-audit-publish** pattern builds each version as an isolated snapshot that no consumer can see, runs every check against it, and advances the catalogue pointer from lesson P3 only if all checks pass. When a check fails, the pointer does not move and consumers carry on with the last good version.

blocks.caption: Write, audit, publish: a version is built in an isolated staging area, audited, and published only by advancing the pointer.

blocks.text: Records that fail an invariant check at ingestion are not dropped. They go to a **quarantine** table (the data equivalent of the dead-letter queue in lesson 17), annotated with the check that rejected them, and they are counted. Once the cause is fixed, quarantined records can be replayed into the next build rather than requested again from the source. The quarantine volume is itself checked: a source whose quarantined records jump from 50 records a night to 50,000 records a night indicates an upstream defect, even if every published record in the primary table is valid.

Blocking a publish has an operational cost, because downstream data becomes 24 hours older. We state the trade-off explicitly. Each dataset has a freshness objective, such as remaining under 48 hours old, and a designated owner authorised to force a publish past a failed check after manual inspection, with the override and its reason recorded. A partial failure raises a second question, and introduces an exception to the rule that the pointer moves only if every check passes. If one region fails and three pass, the pipeline can publish the three and keep the last good version of the fourth. That keeps most of the map fresh, but a version that mixes two days' data can break roads that cross the region boundary. The release manifest records which regions are at which version, allowing consumers that need consistency across regions to wait for a unified release.

The workbench runs thirty nightly builds with four faults (a truncated file, a unit misread, a region missing, and a bug causing gradual road loss) and one legitimate change, where a source adds a country. Each statistical check raises an alert when a region's numbers move further from its baseline than the threshold you set, measured in standard deviations of ordinary night-to-night variation. Find a set of checks and a threshold that stop every fault without a flood of false alarms.

blocks.caption: Thirty nightly builds, four faults and one legitimate change. Each check sees some faults; the threshold trades false alarms against how soon a slow drift is caught.
blocks.task: Stop every fault, with at most one false alarm a month and no alarm for the declared change

blocks.text: No single check catches everything, and the threshold cannot be both low enough to see a slow drift early and high enough to remain quiet on ordinary nights. A blocking check must remain quiet on ordinary nights, which makes it slow to detect subtle drift. A team that wants to see drift sooner adds a separate, more sensitive check that reports to a dashboard rather than blocking the publish.

In lesson 24 we measured services with **service level indicators**, and added three for data products: freshness, completeness and correctness. The checks in this lesson produce those numbers. **Freshness** is the elapsed time since the latest published version was generated, read from the catalogue metadata. **Completeness** is the share of expected records that are present, by region and by source, derived from control totals and per-region counts. **Correctness** is the share of records that match ground truth, which can only be estimated, using the sample audits of lesson P2, comparisons against independent sources, and error reports filed by consumers. Each metric receives an objective, an error budget and an alert, following service indicator practice; the owner of the dataset is paged when an indicator depletes its error budget rapidly.

The Covid spreadsheet failure occurred because of missing operational ownership as much as software limitations; nobody was responsible for checking that the number of results coming out matched the number going in. A data contract names that owner, automated checks enforce the contract, and service level indicators show how well the pipeline meets its agreed targets.

Amazon's Deequ, described by Sebastian Schelter and colleagues in 2018, runs declared checks and computed statistics over very large tables on Apache Spark, keeps the history of each statistic, and flags a value that moves away from its history. Google's TensorFlow Data Validation, described by Eric Breck and colleagues in 2019, infers a schema from data, checks each new batch against it, and compares the distributions of training and serving data, with thresholds on the size of the difference rather than on significance.[^tfdv] Netflix implemented write-audit-publish for its data warehouse using the snapshots of Apache Iceberg: a job writes an unpublished snapshot, the audit runs against it, and publishing advances the table pointer to make it the current snapshot. Iceberg's later branch support performs this pattern by writing to an isolated branch and fast-forwarding the main branch.

Open-source tools such as Great Expectations and dbt's tests let teams write invariant checks as code beside their pipelines, and data catalogues record owners and contracts. The tools are standard. The design work is choosing which checks block a publish, their thresholds, and who may override them.

parts.title: At ten and a hundred times

blocks.text: **At ten times** (hundreds of tables across global regions), engineers cannot write each check by hand. The pipeline profiles each table's history and proposes checks and thresholds, which owners review and accept. Alerts are grouped by root cause, because one broken source can fail dozens of downstream checks in one night, and the owner should receive one grouped alert rather than forty separate pages.

**At a hundred times**, the data contracts become the organisation's map of who depends on whom. Lineage from lesson P3 tells the pipeline which consumers a failed check affects, so the alert goes to them as well as to the producer, and a change to a contract is reviewed by its consumers like a change to an API. Blast radius matters as it did in lesson 23: publishing per region, with independent checks, means a bad source can hold back one region rather than the whole world.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on checking data before it ships
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A partner's contract requires a record count with each daily file of 40,000 records. On one day an import step silently keeps only the first 30,000. Which check catches it on the first day?
choices: A schema check that every field in each loaded record has the right type
A control total sent with the file, compared with the count actually loaded
A distribution check comparing the loaded records with a fixed reference version
items.why: Each of the 30,000 loaded records is valid, and their distribution may look normal. Only a count sent by the producer, compared with the count received, shows that records are missing.

items.ask: A region's road count falls by about 0.2% a night for three weeks because of a bug; its ordinary night-to-night variation is about 1%. A check with a threshold of 3 standard deviations compares each night's count with the average of the previous week and never alarms. Why?
choices: The baseline moves with the drift, so each night looks close to the recent nights before it
The check should use the median of the week, which resists outliers
A week is too short; a month of history would have caught it
items.why: A check against recent history adapts to normal change, and to slow faults too: the count is never more than about 1% below the week's average, which is ordinary noise. A longer window or a median adapts the same way, only more slowly. After three weeks, at 0.2% a night for 21 nights, the count is about 4% below a fixed reference version, which does not adapt, so the drift crosses its threshold.

items.ask: A source is about to add a new country, which will raise the place count by 8% overnight. How should the pipeline handle it?
choices: Raise the volume threshold above 8% for every region, permanently
Switch the volume check off for the night of the change
Let the source's owner declare the change in advance, with its expected effect, so the checks expect it
items.why: Declaring the change keeps the checks as strict as before for everything else. Raising thresholds or switching checks off would also hide a real fault arriving the same night.

items.ask: An audit fails on tonight's build of the map. What do consumers see under write-audit-publish?
choices: The last good version, because the pointer did not move
The new version, with the failing records removed
Nothing at all until the failure has been fixed and the build has passed
items.why: The build is staged in an isolated location, and only a passing audit advances the pointer. Consumers continue reading the last valid version, which is 24 hours older but verified as correct.

items.ask: One region of four fails its checks. The team publishes the other three and keeps the last good version of the fourth. What risk does that create?
choices: None, because each region's data is independent of the others
The three published regions will fail their checks again tomorrow
Data that crosses the region boundary, such as roads, may not match between two days' versions
items.why: Partial publishing keeps most data fresh, but mixes versions. The manifest records which regions are at which version, so consumers that need consistency across regions can wait for a whole version.

items.ask: A road-type feature used to hold about 30 distinct values. After an upstream change it holds 2, though the column exists, has the right type and has the right number of rows, and every pipeline check passes. Which check would have caught it?
choices: A check on the number of rows the feature pipeline produces each day
A check on how many distinct values the feature holds, against its history
A schema check that the feature column exists and has the right type
items.why: The column exists, has the right type and the right number of rows, but its values have collapsed to two, typically a default filled in where a renamed upstream field used to be. A check on the feature's distribution, such as how many distinct values it holds, catches a feature that has silently gone nearly constant.

items.ask: A statistical check alarms whenever a region's numbers move beyond 2 standard deviations. Across four regions and two checks it raises about ten false alarms a month, against a target of about one. What is the likely long-term effect, and the fix?
choices: People learn to override it; raise the threshold, and warn earlier on a dashboard
Little harm, since each alarm costs a day; let each one hold only the affected region
The checks are too many; keep one statistical check at 2 instead of two
items.why: Frequent false alarms train people to ignore or override them, which defeats the gate. Holding one region limits the damage of each alarm but not the habit of overriding, and dropping a check loses the faults only it sees. A blocking check needs a threshold quiet on ordinary nights; earlier warnings can go to a dashboard.

summary: **Bad data fails silently.** A dataset with a region missing or a unit misread looks normal to every reader, so it must be checked before it is published.
**Write a data contract at every handoff.** Schema, meaning and units, freshness, volume and an owner, checked by the producer before it sends anything.
**Send a control total with every delivery.** A count and checksum compared on arrival catches lost records that every other check misses.

**Invariants on records and on the whole version, statistics per region.** Judge statistical checks by the size of a change, against recent history and a fixed reference, and let owners declare expected changes.
**Write, audit, publish.** Build where nobody can read, check, and move the pointer only on a pass; a failed audit leaves consumers on the last good version.
**Quarantine, don't drop.** Rejected records are kept, counted and visible, and the count itself is checked.

**Name the trade-offs.** A blocked publish leaves consumers on data that is right but a day old, so freshness has an objective and an owner who can override on the record; partial publishing mixes versions.
**Measure data like a service.** Freshness, completeness and correctness get objectives, budgets and alerts.

xls.title: Why 65,536
xls.text: The XLS format used by Excel 97 to 2003 numbers rows with 16 bits, so a sheet holds 2¹⁶ = 65,536 rows. The XLSX format introduced with Excel 2007 holds 1,048,576. Within days, Public Health England split the data into smaller batches across more templates.

tfdv.title: Distances, not tests
tfdv.text: TensorFlow Data Validation compares two distributions of a categorical feature by the largest change in the share of any one value (the L-infinity distance), and of a numeric feature by a standard measure of how far apart two histograms are (the Jensen-Shannon divergence). Both measure how different the distributions are. A significance test answers a different question, whether any difference exists, and on a large table it says yes to tiny differences; these distances stay small for small differences however large the table, though on a small table they are noisy.

batch-totals.title: Run-to-run totals
batch-totals.text: Control totals originated in punched-card accounting and early mainframe batch processing in the 1950s. Operators verified run-to-run totals (record counts and arbitrary numeric sums called hash totals) after each card-sorting or magnetic-tape pass before allowing the subsequent batch job in the sequence to run.
